title: Software Quality Mortgage: treating tech debt like a home loan you must repay
summary: Jason Cohen argues that shipping fast with messy code is the right early choice, but it creates tech debt that behaves like a mortgage: you pay interest in bugs and only slowly reduce principal. He explains when to shift from time-to-market to quality and how to win the argument for refactoring with non-technical stakeholders.

principles.text: Early on, ship fast even with bugs; it's the right call while you're still seeking your niche.
principles.quote: When companies are new and unknown, still seeking their niche, the most important thing is to get the software out the door fast, bugs and all.

principles.text: Tech debt works like a mortgage: you borrow to ship v1.0 sooner, then pay interest in bugs without reducing principal.
principles.quote: But eventually you have to pay back the debt. With interest. You pay interest in the form of bugs.

principles.text: Opportunistic cleanup alone never pays it off; growing software is an interest-only mortgage, so allocate real time for major rework.
principles.quote: At some point you can't tolerate this anymore. It's time to pay down the principal in earnest. But this requires allocating time for major rework.

principles.text: Counter 'cleanup is invisible to users': messy code's bugs are visible and slow every new feature.
principles.quote: The bugs constantly produced by messy code are visible to users too. Time spent fixing those bugs could have been spent adding features. The longer we stay in quality debt, the more time it takes to add each new feature.

principles.text: Fix root causes, not symptoms, like pulling weeds up by the roots instead of whacking them weekly.
principles.quote: You'd rather spend your time fixing bugs generated by the problem rather than fixing the problem? That's like whacking weeds every weekend instead of pulling them up by the roots.

principles.text: Don't blame developers for the mess; challenge them to reduce measurable bug reports, and take it seriously when they beg for time to fix bugs.
principles.quote: Finger-pointing impedes resolution. Instead, challenge your developers to reduce bug reports. This is easily measured, so you can track time versus results.
